steps.caption: A fair comparison uses the same whole.
steps.narration: Keep the length representing eighty unchanged. Before and after must use the same scale.

steps.name: Read a percentage change
steps.caption: An increase adds to one hundred percent.
steps.narration: An increase of twenty percent means we keep the original one hundred percent, then add twenty percent of that original amount.

steps.name: Grow the new amount
steps.caption: The green after-bar grows beyond the whole.
steps.narration: The after-bar shows one hundred and twenty percent of the original. The extra twenty percent is a fifth of the original.

steps.name: Calculate the new amount
steps.caption: One hundred and twenty percent of eighty is ninety-six.
steps.narration: Twenty percent of eighty is sixteen. Add it to eighty to get ninety-six units.

steps.name: Name the multiplier
steps.caption: Increase twenty percent means multiply by one point two.
steps.narration: Convert the signed percentage change to a multiplier. One plus zero point two equals one point two. Eighty multiplied by one point two is ninety-six.

data.name: Generalise the repeating pattern
data.caption: A repeated remainder proves a recurring decimal.
data.narration: If a remainder becomes zero, the decimal ends. If a remainder repeats, its digit pattern continues forever.

steps.name: Start with a fraction
steps.caption: Divide the numerator by the denominator.
steps.narration: We begin with one seventh. Decimal division will show us each digit.

steps.name: Find the first remainder
steps.caption: The remainder starts at one.
steps.narration: Seven does not fit into one whole. Start with zero point and use remainder one.

steps.name: Build the first decimal digit
steps.caption: Ten divided by seven gives one remainder three.
steps.narration: Multiply the remainder one by ten. Seven fits once. The next remainder is three.

steps.name: Continue dividing
steps.caption: Each remainder generates one more digit.
steps.narration: Each remainder is multiplied by ten. Divide again, keep the digit and pass the remainder onward.

steps.name: Discover the loop
steps.caption: The original remainder has returned.
steps.narration: Eventually the same remainder returns. That means the same digits will happen again, in exactly the same order.

data.name: Generalise the rule
data.caption: Reduce, factorise, then sort.
data.narration: Only factors two and five in a simplest denominator means terminating. Any other prime factor means recurring.

steps.name: Spot the two types
steps.caption: Some divisions end; others repeat.
steps.narration: We want to discover why some fractions make terminating decimals while others have repeating digits.

steps.name: Reduce first
steps.caption: Always simplify before testing the denominator.
steps.narration: Reduce six fifteenths by three. We get two fifths. It is the denominator of the simplest fraction that matters.

steps.name: Inspect factors
steps.caption: Five is an allowed denominator factor.
steps.narration: The reduced denominator is five. Fractions whose simplified denominators use only twos and fives have terminating decimals.

steps.name: Place a terminating card
steps.caption: Two fifths produces a terminating decimal.
steps.narration: Two fifths is zero point four. Put it in the terminating tray.

steps.name: Find a recurring factor
steps.caption: The factor three remains in one sixth.
steps.narration: Now take one sixth. The denominator still includes a factor of three. Its decimal repeats.
